segments.text: Two headlines, one city.
Rainfall is rising, rainfall is falling.
Both came from the same NASA record.
The difference was the dates.
Over the most recent 15, it points down,
with an interval that includes zero.
Neither chart proves a permanent reversal.
So the engineering question became,
how do we make selective choices visible?
We began with the data.
NASA power provides monthly data from a reanalysis model,
not a neighborhood weather station.
Temperature uses a weighted yearly average.
Rainfall arrives as millimeters per day,
so each rate is multiplied by the days in its month.
Incomplete years are left out.
The original response, retrieval date,
and source hash travel with the analysis.
A polished graph is useful only if its inputs are inspectable.
Then we compared methods.
Ordinary regression gives an understandable baseline.
Adjusted intervals examine correlated errors.
A robust slope checks unusual years.
We tested the candidates on 20,000 synthetic records.
Under strong dependence, none of the deployable candidates
passed every screening case.
So we kept the alternatives visible,
documented their failures,
and avoided presenting one interval as a universal fix.
This is exploration, not forecasting.
The next weakness was date selection.
Four examples help, but they can still hide choices.
The map shows every eligible date window.
Start year on one axis, end year on the other.
Each cell shows its fitted rate.
Select a cell, inspect its observations,
and compare it with another period.
These overlapping estimates are not independent votes,
probabilities, or proof of a climate reversal.
Finally, the result has to survive scrutiny.
Save an investigation with its source response,
settings, and code fingerprint.
Automated tests check calculations and failure paths.
An independent reader can inspect the same inputs
without trusting a screenshot.
Climate Explorer is still a prototype.
The goal is a climate claim that another person can challenge,
